example.problem: You have $5,000 saved, add $200 every month, and expect a 6% annual return. College is 12 years away. How much will you have?
example.title: Saving for college over 12 years

faqs.a: Roughly, with monthly contributions and a 6% return, about $200 a month from birth reaches around $75,000 by age 18. Use this calculator with your own numbers: more time or a higher return lowers the monthly amount you need.
faqs.q: How much should I save each month for college?

faqs.a: Yes, because each contribution earns returns for a different length of time. Money you invest today compounds for the full period, while next year's contributions compound for one year less. That is why starting early matters more than investing more later.
faqs.q: Why does starting early matter so much?

faqs.a: It is a rough long-term average for a mixed stock-and-bond portfolio, but returns are never guaranteed and markets go up and down. Try 4% for a cautious estimate and 7% for an optimistic one, and plan around the cautious number.
faqs.q: Is a 6% return a safe assumption?

faqs.a: A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged account for education in the US: money grows tax-free and withdrawals for qualified education expenses are tax-free too. Many states add a tax deduction for contributions. This calculator's math is the same; the tax treatment is what makes 529s special.

formula.label: Future value
formula.note: P is current savings, PMT the monthly contribution

formula.label: Growth from returns
formula.note: What compounding added on top of what you put in

howItWorks: College savings grow in two ways at once: the money you already have earns returns, and each monthly contribution starts earning returns from the month you add it. The calculator compounds both monthly using the future-value formula: FV = P(1 + i)^n + PMT × ((1 + i)^n − 1) ÷ i, where i is the monthly rate and n the number of months. Because returns themselves earn returns, the growth curve bends upward over time, which is why the last few years add more than the first few.

This is an estimate for planning purposes, not financial advice. Real investment returns vary year to year and are never guaranteed, and taxes and fees also affect the result. A financial advisor can help you pick a savings plan, such as a 529, that fits your situation.
intro: See how much college savings can grow. Enter what you have saved now, your monthly contribution, the expected annual return, and the years until college to get a projected total.

mistakes.text: A 6% annual return is 0.5% a month, not 6% a month. Entering 6 as the monthly rate would inflate the result roughly twelvefold.
mistakes.title: Using the annual rate as the monthly rate

mistakes.text: Contributions made later earn returns for less time. Saving $200 a month for 12 years beats saving $400 a month for 6 years at the same return, because the early money compounds longer.
mistakes.title: Thinking all contributions earn the same returns

mistakes.text: $52,284 in 12 years will not buy what $52,284 buys today. If college costs rise 4% a year, subtract inflation from your expected return to see the result in today's money.
mistakes.title: Ignoring inflation

mistakes.text: Planning around a 9 or 10% return makes the projection look great and the shortfall painful. Run the numbers at 4-5% too, and treat anything above that as a bonus.
mistakes.title: Assuming optimistic returns
